chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subbah al-Kinanī, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

From a man who cursed his wife and disowned her child, then contradicted himself after the mutual cursing (mula'ana) and claimed that the child was indeed his. It was asked: Is it returned to him? He said: 'No, and not even with honor; it is not returned to him, nor is it permissible for him until the Day of Resurrection.'
And regarding the child, who inherits him? He said: 'His mother inherits him.'

I said: 'What if you see that his mother died and he inherited her, then he died? Who inherits him?' He said: 'The paternal uncles of his mother (his mother's paternal uncles), and he inherits his maternal uncles.'

key_terms.الْمُلَاعَنَةِ: Mutual cursing between husband and wife to deny paternity
key_terms.لَعَنَ: Cursed (specifically in the context of Ila)

ai.seo_question: Who inherits a child of Ila if the mother dies before the child?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that if a father performs *ila* and later retracts his denial of paternity, the child remains distinct from his full lineage, inheriting primarily from the mother. Upon the child's death, the inheritance passes to the mother's *asabah* (agnates) and maternal uncles, highlighting the unique legal status of the *ibn al-mula'ana* in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the permanence of the *ila* bond unless explicitly revoked through specific legal mechanisms, preserving the maternal lineage's rights.
